description: Adversaries may abuse PowerShell commands and scripts for execution, leveraging its access to inner Windows functionality.
Adversaries may abuse the Windows command shell (cmd.exe) for execution.
Adversaries may abuse VBScript/Visual Basic scripts for execution.
Adversaries may execute malicious Python scripts to perform actions.
An end user may rely on opening a malicious attachment or file.
Adversaries may abuse the Windows service control manager to execute malicious binaries.
Adversaries may send spearphishing emails with malicious attachments to gain initial access.
Adversaries may send spearphishing emails with malicious links to gain initial access.
Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of existing accounts.
Adversaries may abuse domain accounts to maintain access or evade defenses.
Adversaries may attempt to make an executable or script difficult to analyze.
Adversaries may obfuscate commands to hide intent or bypass string-based detection.
Adversaries may place malicious files in paths associated with legitimate binaries.
Adversaries may inject code into processes in order to evade process-based defenses.
Adversaries may abuse task scheduling functionality to facilitate initial or recurring execution.
Adversaries may achieve persistence by adding entries to Windows Registry Run keys.
Adversaries may create or modify Windows services to execute malicious commands on system boot.
Adversaries may attempt to access credential material stored in LSASS memory.
Adversaries may attempt to access or copy the Active Directory domain database (ntds.dit).
Adversaries may attempt to systematically guess passwords against accounts.
Adversaries may use a single common password against many accounts to avoid lockouts.
Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of domain accounts.
Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of other systems by name or IP.
Adversaries may seek detailed information about the operating system and hardware.
Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of services running on remote hosts.
Adversaries may use valid RDP credentials to connect remotely to internal hosts.
Adversaries may use SMB to interact with administrative shares for lateral movement.
Adversaries may transfer tools or files into an compromised internal network.
Adversaries may communicate using application layer web protocols (HTTP/HTTPS).
Adversaries may communicate using DNS protocol for C2 or data tunneling.
Adversaries may encrypt data on target systems to interrupt availability (Ransomware).
Adversaries may delete or disable shadow copies or backup configurations to hinder recovery.
Adversaries may exfiltrate data over alternative non-C2 protocols.
Adversaries may exfiltrate data directly to cloud storage services.
